claims.text: The initial material is a coarse-surfaced, native unoxidized CoCrFeMnNi protective coating.
During sliding, environmental oxygen reacts with CoCrFeMnNi and induces tribo-oxidation.
The sliding-induced interfacial film is an oxide.
Sliding can form an ultra-nanocrystalline or near-amorphous surface film in CoCrFeMnNi.
The oxygen-derived oxide film dynamically regenerates during sliding.
The ultra-nanocrystalline surface film reduces wear.
The film reduces wear by acting as a protective oxide barrier.
The ultra-nanocrystalline surface film is associated with reduced friction.
The oxide film lowers friction through a lubricating mechanism.
The oxide film increases surface hardness through an inverse Hall-Petch effect.
CoCrFeMnNi can exhibit inverse Hall-Petch behavior in its highly refined worn near-surface layer.
An inert or ultra-high-vacuum environment minimizes oxidation and mixed metal-oxide film formation.
Suppressing the oxide film in an inert environment produces higher wear than testing in oxygen-rich air.
Suppressing the oxide film in an inert environment produces higher friction than testing in oxygen-rich air.
Oxygen-rich testing will produce a TEM/EDS-detectable ultra-nanocrystalline oxide layer.
Oxygen-rich testing will significantly reduce the wear rate relative to inert testing.
Oxygen-rich testing will significantly reduce the friction coefficient relative to inert testing.
The proposed atmospheric effect should hold for CoCrFeMnNi coatings under moderate sliding loads and speeds when temperature and kinetic factors are controlled.
Sliding-induced temperature changes can affect oxidation rates.
Differences in alloy processing history can alter oxidation behavior.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts that oxidation improves wear resistance and friction and that inert testing performs worse, whereas both cited records report low friction and high wear resistance in oxidation-mitigating inert or UHV conditions; the results record explicitly characterizes oxidation-producing environments as detrimental.

The proposed mediator is an ultra-nanocrystalline oxide film, but the cited same-system evidence attributes performance to a shear-refined, near-amorphous layer formed on bare alloy while oxide formation was mitigated.

The conditions state that only oxygen availability should differ, but the suggested comparison of ambient air with ultra-high vacuum also changes total pressure and interfacial gas environment; this is avoided only if a pressure-matched inert-gas control is used.
